claims.statement: This reference covers FPT, GHEC and GHES; version-specific sections and navigation are not evidence of deployed security.
Transformed secrets may evade redaction; repository write users can access secrets. Use least-privilege credentials and read-only token defaults with only necessary job-scoped elevation.

Do not embed sensitive plaintext in workflow files; mask non-GitHub secrets. Runner redaction requires a secret to be used within the job and accessible to the runner, but is not guaranteed; exposure calls for source-recommended log deletion and rotation subject to actual custody and owner authority.
Avoid structured secret blobs because exact-match redaction is less reliable; individual values improve matching.
Register generated sensitive values and transformations as secrets; transformations are not automatically safe in logs.
Review workflow/action code for unintended destinations and inspect stdout/stderr with both valid and invalid inputs; successful runs alone do not establish secrecy.
Periodically review whether secrets remain needed, remove unnecessary secrets and rotate; this is upstream guidance, not a performed rotation.
Environment required reviewers can withhold secret access pending approval; this does not establish runner isolation.
An action argument avoids generating an inline script from untrusted expressions; the mutable example tag is illustrative and needs independent action review.
Intermediate environment variables and quoted shell expansion mitigate expression-to-script injection; action and shell boundaries still need review.
The FPT/GHEC CodeQL workflow-template references describe optional analysis setup, not installed scanning or acceptance.
Consider restricting GITHUB_TOKEN permissions; actual effective job authority requires a separate check.
Privileged pull_request_target and workflow_run jobs must not execute untrusted fork content; untrusted checkout, shared caches and workflow_run artifacts require explicit trust-boundary review.
CodeQL and Scorecard are suggested analysis aids; references alone do not prove comprehensive detection.
Compromised actions may reach job credentials and interact with other jobs through files, environment or Docker sockets; review actual secret availability rather than infer universal access.
Full-length commit SHAs are described as immutable references, subject to the stated collision qualification; verify origin in the action repository, not a fork.
Optional SHA/blocklist policy capability is feature-gated: FPT/GHEC and GHES >=3.19; configuration availability is not activation.
Audit selected action source for intended secret handling and absence of unintended log/host disclosure.
If trusting tags, creator identity can inform selection, but tags remain mutable and a verified creator badge is not code-safety proof.
Apply action immutability and source-review principles to third-party reusable workflows.
Built-in security features and workflow CODEOWNERS monitoring are review options; a CODEOWNERS entry alone does not establish required approval.
Custom organization Actions roles separate policy, runner, secret and variable management; the feature is GHEC and GHES >=3.14, not universal access.
OIDC can replace long-lived cloud secrets where supported; this pin states AWS does not support custom claims, so provider trust capabilities require explicit review.
Dependabot version updates can maintain action and reusable-workflow references; this does not establish installed configuration.

GHEC/GHES private/internal action sharing permits indirect outside-collaborator access to run logs; its scoped read installation token expires after one hour and is distinct from other workflow credentials.
Automated creation/approval of pull requests can bypass intended oversight; review enterprise, organization and repository settings rather than infer approval authority.
CodeQL and optional Scorecard checks cover common insecure workflow patterns; installation, coverage and result freshness remain unproved.
GHES requires self-hosted runners; hosted-runner security and architecture links in the following section are FPT/GHEC guidance.

On FPT/GHEC the actions-sbom feature exposes maintained hosted-image SBOM release assets for Ubuntu, Windows, macOS and ARM; vulnerability scanning or build inclusion is optional and not performed here.
Hosted-runner hosts files block specified mining/malicious hosts; this is not a general egress isolation guarantee.

FPT/GHEC hosted runners are described as clean ephemeral environments; self-hosted runners lack that guarantee and should almost never serve public repositories. Private/internal untrusted forks remain hazardous.
Environment approval does not isolate self-hosted runners; owners can restrict repository-level creation, subject to platform and management-role scope.
Shared runners can spread compromise across repositories; runner groups and available workflow restrictions must follow trust boundaries, with workflow restriction availability GHEC/GHES.

Review resident credentials, network services and metadata endpoints on self-hosted runners; minimize sensitive information in the environment and recognize that any user able to invoke workflows may reach that information.
Destroy-after-job schemes need verified cleanup and may still run multiple jobs; concurrent process arguments can expose credentials.
JIT registration limits a runner to at most one job before removal, but reused hardware still needs a clean environment.
The encoded JIT launch configuration is an illustration, not a runner installation or registration authorization.
Choose runner-management level by shared ownership and isolation needs; enterprise/organization centralization and repository overhead tradeoffs are contextual, not a universal estate design.

For cloud deployment or intended HashiCorp Vault authentication, the source recommends considering OIDC to obtain short-lived, well-scoped tokens; this conditional recommendation is not a general provider deployment or measured lifetime guarantee.
User security logs and organization/conditional enterprise audit logs expose different review scopes; the secret-update screenshot and action filter are examples, not actual audit evidence.

The dependency graph describes uses at step/job levels, versions/SHAs and known advisories. The source spells ./github/workflows/ here; local tooling uses .github/workflows/. Platform enablement differs between public/private FPT/GHEC and GHES enterprise setup.
The advisory database supports Actions filtering; marketplace or known advisory review does not cover unknown vulnerabilities.
Dependabot alerts inspect default-branch known vulnerable actions, but only semantic-version references receive these alerts; SHA pinning is not evidence of automatic alert coverage.
Dependabot alerts and dependency-review diffs/actions can inform rejection of introduced vulnerable versions; the linked tools are not configured by this review.
Version updates target the latest action version while security updates target the minimum patched version; they solve different maintenance needs.
Action-update support excludes local and Docker URL references; same-line version comments and untagged-commit update behavior need explicit maintenance review.
FPT/GHEC action publishers can inspect dependents and coordinate advisories in private forks; these are conditional publishing capabilities, not permission to redistribute reviewed sources.

scope: Full pinned article and literal closure read; source propositions are reference-only and do not adopt policy.
